To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The design of an object-oriented system is the result of a rule development process that is performed by the designer in a rule space and in an instance space.

(1) the initial representation of a problem in object-oriented design is based on the problem statement, but (2) it is refined and/or changed during rule development to correspond to knowledge acquired during rule development.

(a) internal representations of problems in the early stages of OOD are based on the problem statement, (b) rule development is a two-stage process in which the rule space is used to build rules and the instance space is used to simulate instances, (c) the rule space is the locus of rule development, and (d) rule development is an iterative process in which the initial representation is refined as new knowledge is gained.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how designers build representations, and how they use these representations to construct and refine design rules and objects.
how designers build internal representations and how they develop rules.
the cognitive aspects of rule development and representation in object-oriented design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the internal representation and rule development framework can be used as a tool for studying and teaching object-oriented design.
the cognitive framework proposed in this study provides an adequate description of the process of rule development in OOD, but it is not a sufficient description.
object-oriented development is an activity of developing rules and building internal representations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cognitive framework we have developed can be used to explain and predict differences in rule development processes and the resulting designs in OOD.

the design process is a process that involves the construction and refinement of an internal representation of a problem, and the construction and refinement (or modification) of the internal representation is done through the construction and refinement or modification of rules.
the internal representations and rule development process in OOD are strongly related and can be used to predict the final design.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the internal representations and the rules that are built during OOD are not only a function of the problem, but also of the designer.
rule development is not just a cognitive process but also a process of representation development.
OOD is a complex process involving the development of both rules and representations.
